questions.q: In a partnership, how is equity typically shared?
options: Equally among all employees
It cannot be shared; only one person can own equity
According to an agreement among two or more owners
Partnerships do not have equity
questions.explain: A partnership has two or more owners who share profits, losses, and equity according to a partnership agreement.

questions.q: Which of these groups would rely on financial information to decide whether to extend MORE credit to a business?
options: The company's competitors
Random members of the public
Lenders and creditors
Nobody — lenders never look at financial records
questions.explain: Lenders and creditors read financial information to judge whether a business can repay what it borrows before extending more credit.

questions.q: In the accounting equation, what does Equity represent?
options: The owners' residual claim on the business after liabilities are subtracted from assets
The total amount of cash the business has on hand
Everything the business owes to outside parties
A tax the business must pay each year
questions.explain: Equity is what's left for the owners once everything owed to outsiders (liabilities) is subtracted from everything the business owns (assets).

questions.q: Why are Liabilities, Equity, and Revenue all credit-normal?
options: Because they are the least important accounts
Because credit-normal accounts are always larger in dollar amount
Because they all sit on the right-hand side of, or increase, the right-hand side of the accounting equation (Assets = Liabilities + Equity)
There is no underlying reason; it is simply arbitrary tradition
questions.explain: Liabilities and Equity sit on the right side of the accounting equation and naturally increase on the credit side; Revenue increases Equity, so it behaves the same way.

questions.q: What do the words "debit" and "credit" fundamentally mean in accounting?
options: Debit always means a decrease, credit always means an increase
Debit means the left side of an account, credit means the right side
Debit is for expenses only, credit is for revenue only
Debit means good news, credit means bad news
questions.explain: Debit and credit are simply positional labels: left side and right side of an account. Whether they increase or decrease a balance depends on account type.

questions.q: What would it typically suggest if a company's Cash account showed a credit balance?
options: A likely recording error, since Cash is debit-normal and shouldn't normally sit on the credit side
Nothing unusual — this is completely normal for Cash
That the company has too much cash on hand
That the company is a corporation rather than a partnership
questions.explain: A credit balance in a debit-normal account like Cash is usually a red flag worth investigating for an error.

options: The increase in equity resulting from a business's ordinary, core operating activities
Cash received from any source, including loans
A type of liability owed to customers
The total amount of inventory a business has sold at cost
questions.explain: Revenue is the increase in equity that comes specifically from a business's core operations, like selling goods or services.

questions.q: Why can a business record a leased piece of equipment as an asset, even though it does not legally own it?
options: Because leased equipment is always classified as a liability instead
Because the asset definition is based on control, not strict legal ownership
Because leases are never recorded in accounting at all
Because only purchased equipment counts, and leases are an exception with no rule
questions.explain: The asset definition hinges on control of the resource, not necessarily outright legal ownership.

questions.q: What does the matching principle say about when an expense should be recorded?
options: Always in the period the cash is paid, no exceptions
Only at the end of the fiscal year
In the same period as the revenue it helped generate, regardless of when it was paid for
Expenses are never matched to any particular period
questions.explain: The matching principle requires expenses to be recorded in the same period as the revenue they helped produce.

questions.q: If a trial balance's difference divides evenly by 9, what type of error does that suggest?
options: A missing journal entry with no error otherwise
A transposition error, where two digits were swapped while keying an amount
A duplicate payment to a vendor
An error that can never actually be diagnosed
questions.explain: Transposition errors (swapping two adjacent digits) always produce a difference evenly divisible by 9.

questions.q: What does the Oracle Fusion Subledger Accounting engine fundamentally do, in terms of this lesson's concepts?
options: It eliminates the need for journal entries entirely
It only handles compound entries, never simple ones
It is a rules engine that turns subledger transactions into correctly formed journal entries with this same date/debit/credit/memo anatomy
It has no relationship to journal entries at all
questions.explain: Subledger Accounting takes transactions from subledgers like Payables and Receivables and turns them into properly structured journal entries behind the scenes.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of a subledger in Oracle Fusion Financials?
options: General Ledger itself
The chart of accounts
Accounts Payable
The accounting equation
questions.explain: Accounts Payable (along with Receivables and Fixed Assets) is a subledger that tracks detailed, process-specific transactions before summarizing into the GL.

questions.q: What is the core revenue recognition principle?
options: Revenue is recognized whenever cash is received, regardless of delivery
Revenue is recognized only at the end of the fiscal year
Revenue is recognized when control of a good or service transfers to the customer, in the amount the business expects to be entitled to receive
Revenue is recognized before any contract is signed
questions.explain: The core principle ties revenue recognition to the transfer of control, not to the timing of cash.

questions.q: A customer pays $12,000 upfront for a year of subscription service that hasn't been delivered yet. Which category does this fall into?
options: Accrued Revenue
Accrued Expense
Prepaid Expense
Deferred (Unearned) Revenue
questions.explain: Cash has already been collected, but the revenue has not yet been earned — this is Deferred (Unearned) Revenue.

questions.q: What is the difference between a 'closed' period and a 'permanently closed' period?
options: A closed period can potentially be reopened for a genuine correction; a permanently closed period is locked for good
There is no difference; the terms are interchangeable
A permanently closed period can still accept new transactions
A closed period has never had any transactions posted to it
questions.explain: Closed periods can sometimes be reopened if truly needed, while permanently closed periods are locked with no realistic expectation of reopening.

questions.q: Which of the three cash flow statement categories includes buying new equipment?
options: Operating activities
Investing activities
Financing activities
None of the three categories cover equipment purchases
questions.explain: Investing activities cover cash spent on or received from long-term assets, such as purchasing equipment.

questions.q: What happens to revenue and expense accounts specifically at year-end that does NOT happen at a routine month-end close?
options: They are permanently deleted from the chart of accounts
They are closed (zeroed out), with their net effect rolled into Retained Earnings
They are converted into liabilities
Nothing different happens to them at year-end
questions.explain: At year-end, temporary accounts (revenue and expenses) are closed into Retained Earnings so the next fiscal year starts with a fresh income statement.

questions.q: What does the income statement report?
options: A business's revenues and expenses over a period of time, resulting in net income or net loss
A business's assets and liabilities at a single point in time
Only a business's cash balance
A business's stock price history
questions.explain: The income statement reports revenue and expenses over a stretch of time (a month, quarter, or year), netting down to net income or net loss.
